entities.label: Place
entities.summary:
Ancient Carthage, a formidable Phoenician city-state and later a dominant maritime empire, emerged on the Gulf of Tunis's eastern shore (modern Tunisia) around 813 BCE, traditionally founded by Queen Dido (Elissa). It rapidly evolved from a trading post into the preeminent naval and commercial power of the Western Mediterranean by the 4th century BCE, challenging Greek and later Roman hegemony. Its strategic location at the crossroads of major trade routes between Africa, Europe, and Asia Minor allowed it to control vast resources and influence political developments across the ancient world, particularly through its vast network of colonies and trading factories. Carthage's distinctive blend of Phoenician maritime prowess, sophisticated mercantile economy, and military innovation, including its reliance on mercenary forces led by brilliant generals like Hannibal Barca, made it a unique and enduring rival to the nascent Roman Republic.

At its zenith, the Carthaginian Empire encompassed territories from North Africa (modern Tunisia, Algeria, Libya) to southern Iberia, Sardinia, Corsica, and western Sicily. Its wealth derived from controlling trans-Saharan gold routes, silver mines in Iberia, and extensive agricultural lands producing grain, olives, and wine. The city itself boasted a population estimated at 400,000 by the 3rd century BCE, featuring monumental architecture, advanced harbor facilities (the Cothon), and a complex political system blending aristocratic and democratic elements. The First Punic War (264–241 BCE) saw Carthage's naval supremacy challenged by Rome, leading to the loss of Sicily. The Second Punic War (218–201 BCE), famously spearheaded by Hannibal's audacious crossing of the Alps, brought Rome to the brink of collapse but ultimately ended in Carthaginian defeat at Zama, largely due to Scipio Africanus's strategic brilliance.
